summary: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion service now supports time series collections in the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as a pipeline destination. You can stream logs, metrics, traces and event data into time series collections with fully managed pipelines. You don't have to run your own collectors or write custom ingestion code. OpenSearch Ingestion delivers data from the sources you already use, including OpenTelemetry, Amazon S3, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK, Amazon DynamoDB, and HTTP endpoints. Before indexing, pipelines can filter, enrich, transform, and route data with built-in processors. For example, you can parse and normalize log fields, mask sensitive data, or split a stream into separate indexes. Pipelines scale automatically with your workload. Time series collections add a lower-cost warm storage tier and built-in alerting and anomaly detection. title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers free monthly web search queries
summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers 5,000 free web search queries per month through the Web Search Tool in AgentCore gateway and the Web Search API. AgentCore helps developers build, deploy, and operate highly effective agents securely at scale. When new AWS Config managed rules map to the framework's controls, or when the framework itself is revised, AWS updates your deployed pack automatically. Because AWS maintains a consistent pack definition in every supported Region, you can deploy the same framework across Regions without building or maintaining Region-specific rule sets. With managed conformance packs you no longer have to track framework changes or update rules yourself. Previously, to evaluate resources against a framework such as PCI DSS or SOC 2, you started from a sample conformance pack template, customized it for your environment, and then updated it yourself whenever new rules became available or the framework changed. title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now offers SQL statement statistics in Database Insights
summary: Amazon Aurora DSQL now records statistics for each SQL statement your cluster runs and publishes them as Amazon CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics. You can view them in Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights. For each statement, you see how often it runs, how long it takes, the rows it scans, returns, or changes, and the DPUs it uses. Statement statistics measure every successful statement rather than sampling activity. Use them to find the statements that take the most time, run most often, or cost the most. In Database Insights, choose a statement under Top SQL to see its normalized SQL text and per-call charts. You can also query the metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch. Turn on statement statistics for each cluster in the Aurora DSQL console or the API when you create or update the cluster. title: Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor now helps you find issues before your users notice them (Public Preview)
summary: When a WorkSpace is slow or won't connect, the IT administrator trying to help has traditionally had to dig through Amazon CloudWatch metrics, logs, and configuration data across multiple tools to find out why. And in the meantime, the user on the other end can't get their work done. In April this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor, an AI-powered agent that helps IT administrators diagnose and fix WorkSpaces performance, connectivity and provisioning issues and get users back to work faster. With Advisor, administrators can investigate a WorkSpace from the console and, in minutes, see the likely root cause and recommended actions they can take right away. Since then, we've continued to invest in Advisor so your team can spend less time chasing down issues one by one, and more time on the projects your business is counting on you to deliver. title: Amazon VPC, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN now offer a 99.999% availability SLA for cross-Region traffic
summary: AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a new capability called Multipath Resilience. Multipath Resilience makes it easier to improve the resilience of mission-critical applications that send traffic across Regions, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming. The AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths. When a path fails, such as during a fiber cut, the network's automatic sub-second rerouting moves traffic to a healthy path. In the rare event that such mechanisms do not resolve the issue in a timely manner, such as when there's a partial degradation, it might take minutes for connectivity to be reestablished. title: Amazon MSK Standard Brokers now support Graviton4-based M8g instances
service: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka
summary: AWS Graviton4-based M8g instances are now generally available for Standard Brokers in Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK). title: Amazon S3 now provides post-quantum TLS visibility in AWS CloudTrail
summary: Amazon S3 now records the TLS key exchange algorithm in AWS CloudTrail for S3 requests, so you can see which requests and clients use post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS). With this visibility, you can measure the share of your S3 traffic that is protected with post-quantum cryptography, and identify the applications, SDK versions, and IAM principals that still connect with classical key exchange and need to be upgraded. The new keyExchange value in the tlsDetails field of CloudTrail management and data events shows the key exchange negotiated on each TLS connection, such as the hybrid post-quantum algorithm X25519MLKEM768 or a traditional algorithm such as x25519. For example, you can query your CloudTrail logs to find the user agents of S3 requests that did not use ML-KEM, then prioritize those clients for your post-quantum migration. title: Amazon S3 adds post-quantum TLS key exchange support to additional S3 endpoints
summary: Amazon S3 adds post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS) key exchange support to S3 Vectors and AWS PrivateLink for Amazon S3 interface endpoints. This extends the post-quantum cryptography support already available on regional S3, S3 Tables, and S3 Express One Zone endpoints. S3 Vectors endpoints and PrivateLink interface endpoints now support Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), one of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. PQ-TLS key exchange is available to all clients configured to use the ML-KEM key exchange algorithm. S3 Vectors and PrivateLink endpoints automatically negotiate the strongest key exchange that your client software supports, so clients that support ML-KEM receive the benefits of PQ-TLS key exchange without any changes to your applications or endpoint configuration. PQ-TLS key exchange for S3 Vectors and AWS PrivateLink for S3 is supported at no additional cost in all AWS Regions. To learn

title: Cost Optimization Hub now supports stopping idle Amazon EC2 instances
summary: AWS Cost Optimization Hub now lets you stop idle Amazon EC2 instances directly from your recommendations. Cost Optimization Hub consolidates and prioritizes cost optimization recommendations across your AWS accounts and Regions, including idle resources. Previously, stopping an idle instance required you to leave Cost Optimization Hub and identify the specific instance in the Amazon EC2 console. Now you can stop it from the Savings opportunities page in Cost Optimization Hub. When you choose Stop next to an idle instance recommendation, a confirmation shows the instance, its account and Region, what the instance loses when it stops, such as instance store data and data in memory, and what continues to bill, such as EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses. Stopping does not terminate the instance or delete its EBS volumes, and you can start it again from the EC2 console. Stop needs no separate setup and uses your existing permissions. title: AWS WAF announces simplified onboarding for Bot Control targeted protection
summary: Today, AWS WAF announces a simplified console experience for Bot Control at the targeted inspection level. A single setting, Targeted bot control, turns on targeted protection for your Amazon CloudFront distributions with the configuration AWS recommends. It comes with two additions to the Bot Control managed rule group: bot confidence levels, which summarize the targeted detections on each request as High, Medium, or Low, and a LATEST version that keeps you on the newest detections automatically. Together, they help you protect your applications against sophisticated and AI-powered bots without writing label match rules or changing application code. The targeted inspection level uses machine learning and client-side signals to detect evasive bots. Previously, acting on those signals meant integrating the AWS WAF JavaScript SDK into every page, learning dozens of labels, and writing label match rules to combine them. Now, the rule group combines the detections into one confidence level

title: AWS Transit Gateway supports native integration with Gateway Load Balancer
summary: AWS Transit Gateway now supports network function attachments of type Gateway Load Balancer, simplifying the deployment and management of network security across your AWS network. With a network function attachment, you can connect your transit gateway to a Gateway Load Balancer VPC endpoint service that fronts firewalls and other security appliances without complex VPC configurations. Transit Gateway creates and manages the Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in the Availability Zones you choose, removing the need to create dedicated endpoint subnets and route tables. The endpoint service can be in another AWS account. Network function attachments also support context sharing with security services. Transit Gateway adds resource context to traffic sent to your firewall, including the transit gateway attachment, VPC, subnet, and security groups. Your firewall can use this context alongside IP addresses to enforce segmentation policies. This capability is available in all commercial AWS Reg

title: AWS Transit Gateway now shares resource context with firewalls for segmentation policies
summary: AWS Transit Gateway now supports context sharing with security services, such as attached firewalls, allowing you to use Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), VPC subnets, VPC security groups, and transit gateway attachments in firewall policies alongside IP addresses. Until now, attached firewalls segmented traffic by IP address, which is hard to plan and maintain, or by resource tags, which firewalls periodically synchronize with IP addresses and can miss new workloads in between. With this feature, you can enforce segmentation based on how workloads and attachments are defined in AWS. Transit Gateway embeds resource context in the traffic it sends to your firewall, which can enforce the right policy from the first packet. For example, you can apply threat protection to traffic between web-tier and database-tier security groups, block development VPCs from reaching production VPCs, apply a common inspection policy to traffic entering AWS through AWS Direct Connect and AWS Site-to-Sit

title: AWS Transform now supports migration to AWS Outposts
summary: AWS Transform now supports AWS Outposts as a migration target. You can migrate workloads onto your Outposts from on-premises environments, another Outpost, or a different Availability Zone or Region. AWS Transform is a collaborative enterprise IT transformation service powered by agentic AI that accelerates cloud migration, application modernization, and continuous tech debt reduction. Run your migration with AI agents in AWS Transform for migrations, or use AWS Transform MGN , the rehost engine within AWS Transform, directly from its console. If you run workloads on Outposts for low latency, local data processing, or data residency, migrating them has meant manual effort or legacy tooling, often with a detour through the Region and an AMI copy. Now you choose subnets on the Outpost for your migration, and AWS Transform continuously replicates your source servers at the block level, directly from your source environment to the Outpost. You launch test instances before cutover and cut o

title: AWS Transform now provides Well-Architected Agent reviews
summary: AWS Transform for migrations now includes Well-Architected reviews of target networks as it migrates and modernizes infrastructure to AWS. These recommendations, provided by the AWS Well-Architected Agent in public preview, are based on the latest best practices across security, reliability, and cost optimization pillars, and are applied directly to your target network, so you don't have to update the infrastructure after deployment on AWS. While migrating networks, design gaps typically surface after deployment, making fixes costly, requiring separate review and update cycles. For teams migrating large on-premises networks, this capability catches improvement opportunities early in the planning stage. AWS Well-Architected Agent provides recommendations, such as re-addressing spoke VPCs using non-RFC1918 addresses and governing CIDR allocation, and AWS Transform applies them to the network design. Post-deployment recommendations are documented for you as downloadable artifact from AWS

title: AWS Split Cost Allocation Data now supports Amazon S3
summary: Starting today, you can allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to the prefixes in that bucket in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Organizations often store data for many teams, applications, or tenants in one bucket under different prefixes, such as `marketing/` and `finance/`. Until now, attributing that bucket's bill to each prefix required custom pipelines built on S3 Inventory or Storage Lens reports and your own pricing logic. With Split Cost Allocation Data for Amazon S3, Amazon S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management, which allocates the bucket's storage and Tier 1 and Tier 2 request costs to the deepest matching prefix in the range of prefix levels you choose. Each prefix line item carries its full prefix path as AWS-generated cost allocation tags, so you can total cost by top-level prefix, team, or application, and reconcile it back to the bucket. You can use this dat

title: AWS Split Cost Allocation Data now supports Amazon S3
summary: You can now allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to its prefixes in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Many organizations store data for multiple teams, applications, or tenants in one bucket under different prefixes such as "marketing/" and "finance/". Previously, splitting that bucket's bill by prefix required custom pipelines and your own pricing logic. With this new capability, S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management. Billing and Cost Management then allocates the bucket's storage and Tier 1 and Tier 2 request costs to the deepest matching prefix in the range of prefix levels you choose. Each prefix line item carries its full prefix path as AWS-generated cost allocation tags, so you can total costs by top-level prefix, team, or application, and reconcile it back to the bucket. You can use this data for chargeback and showback, and to see which prefixes drive your S3 spend.

title: AWS Lambda durable functions now supports pausing and deleting executions
summary: AWS Lambda durable functions now lets you pause a running durable execution and resume it later without losing its progress. When you resume an execution, it continues from its last checkpoint on the same function version. By default, time spent paused doesn't count toward the execution timeout. You can also now delete a completed execution's data before its retention period ends. With Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. With this launch, when a downstream service is degraded or a model provider's rate limit is reached, you can pause affected executions while you resolve the issue instead of letting the retries run out. You can also delete an execution's history, checkpoint data, and input and output payloads after it succeeds, fails, stops, or times out. For example, you can delete an execution whose input contains personal data, or clean up failed exe

title: AWS IAM announces Access Troubleshooter to debug access denied errors
summary: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) introduces Access Troubleshooter , a new capability that gives you visibility into the full authorization context behind access denied errors so you can resolve them without trial-and-error. Previously, developers relied on the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the denying policy to debug a denial, with no visibility into the authorization context or other policies evaluated in the request that could contribute to the denial. This made troubleshooting access issues time-consuming and inefficient. Starting today, access denied error messages for supported services and APIs will include a unique identifier that you can use to retrieve details of the authorization performed by the service. You gain visibility into what policies were evaluated for each request, the authorization context of those requests, and the results of the evaluation. This enables you to identify the root cause of authorization issues quickly, streamlining your access management wo

title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports cluster operations for tracking scaling and on-demand Deep Health Check requests
summary: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod introduces cluster operations, giving you visibility into every scaling and on-demand deep health check request from submission to completion. When a request runs into errors, the SageMaker AI console shows an alert that links directly to that request's error events. With continuous provisioning, HyperPod brings capacity online in the background as it becomes available, retries failed nodes automatically, and lets you run multiple scaling requests at the same time. Cluster operations show you when each request finishes and which request caused the activity on your cluster. When a scale-up falls short of its target, you can go directly to the failure reason. Each scaling or on-demand deep health check request creates a cluster operation that tracks the request from submission to completion, including whether it is still in progress and what it changed on each instance group. Events that HyperPod records while working on the request are linked to its operation.

title: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now supports Infoblox Threat Defense (Preview)
summary: Amazon Web Services announces the preview of Infoblox Threat Defense on Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall . Security administrators can now apply Infoblox threat intelligence directly in DNS Firewall rules to preemptively protect applications in their Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) from cyber threats, by subscribing to the Infoblox product listing on AWS Marketplace from the Route 53 DNS Firewall console. With this launch, you can add Infoblox managed rules to your DNS Firewall rule groups to filter and block queries to malicious and high-risk domains at the DNS layer. Infoblox continuously updates its threat intelligence feeds to preemptively protect cloud workloads from phishing, malware, ransomware and other advanced attacks. You can apply these protections to DNS queries from your VPCs and to hybrid traffic forwarded through Route 53 Resolver endpoints, so security teams keep consistent DNS policies across AWS and on-premises environments and add a layer of protection on

title: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now supports automated allow-list generation
summary: Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now automatically generates domain allow-lists from your VPCs' observed DNS query traffic, helping you enforce least-privilege DNS access and reduce the risk of DNS-based data exfiltration. Previously, implementing a least-privilege model required security teams to manually analyze DNS query logs to identify the domains their VPCs depend on before deploying allow-list rules. This created operational overhead and delayed enforcement of a deny-by-default (walled-garden) posture. With automated allow-list generation, DNS Firewall analyzes DNS query traffic using a lookback window configurable from 1 hour to 7 days to create an allow-list of observed domains. It then continuously monitors DNS queries and flags newly observed domains, so you can review them before adding them to the allow-list. You can deploy the rule across multiple VPCs and accounts using AWS Firewall Manager or Route 53 Profiles. This capability is available at no additional cost to

title: Amazon Route 53 Global Resolver is now available over AWS Cloud WAN for hybrid networks
summary: Amazon Route 53 Global Resolver now supports anycast DNS resolution for private connections managed through your AWS Cloud WAN configuration. This enables organizations with hybrid networks to resolve DNS queries to public and private domains over existing AWS Direct Connect or AWS VPN connections, with automatic multi-region failover for high availability. Previously, customers had to either deploy and manage separate Resolver endpoints in each AWS Region and customer location, with no automatic failover between AWS Regions, or use Global Resolver with internet-reachable anycast IPs, making it hard for clients without internet access or those restricted by compliance requirements to take advantage of Global Resolver's anycast DNS resolution. With this launch, customers with clients configured with private connectivity over your Cloud WAN network get all the benefits of Global Resolver: automatic regional failover for higher availability, centralized DNS filtering with Route 53 DNS Fir

title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams announces queues to simplify and reduce costs of real-time processing
summary: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports queues, a simpler and more cost-effective way to process a stream. Because queues track the delivery state of each record, your consumer instances receive records instead of leasing shards, acknowledge each record when processing is complete, and scale beyond the number of shards. Kinesis Data Streams consumers can reduce the cost of processing data by up to 43% by using queues instead of the Kinesis Client Library. You no longer run a DynamoDB table or custom metrics, and you use compute more efficiently. Queues in Kinesis Data Streams are powered by Amazon SQS. Built on that foundation, a queue delivers records at least once, redelivers records your consumers do not acknowledge, and provides built-in dead-letter handling for records that keep failing. Each queue publishes its own CloudWatch metrics, so you can scale consumer instances on records waiting to be received and alarm on records that repeatedly fail. Use queues for applications that

title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now rightsizes Pods to reduce compute costs (Preview)
summary: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) introduces resource optimization for EKS Auto Mode, a new capability that rightsizes the CPU and memory requests of running Pods based on their actual usage. CPU and memory requests are often set at deploy time and rarely revisited, and Auto Mode provisions EC2 instances to fit them. Rightsizing lets Auto Mode run the same Deployments and StatefulSets on fewer or smaller instances, without hand tuning and at no additional charge. Turn on resource optimization by creating a ClusterResourceOptimizationPolicy in your EKS cluster, review its recommendations in the default Recommend mode, and switch to Apply mode when you're ready to resize running Pods in place, without recreating them. For example, a platform team running Java services under Argo CD can rightsize every application namespace without editing templates or creating GitOps drift, while resource optimization keeps memory above each Java heap and raises memory after an out-of-memory

title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports case and calculated template variables
summary: Amazon Connect Customer message templates, which personalize each message with details about its recipient, now support case fields from Cases and calculated attributes from Customer Profiles, such as a customer's most frequent contact channel. Companies that send updates about a claim, an order, or an application need each message to reflect that customer's record. Template authors can insert case fields, including custom fields that administrators define, and Connect Customer fills in the current value for each recipient every time it sends a message that uses the template. A claims manager at an insurance company can build one email template that pulls each claim's reference number and status from its case, so every policyholder receives an update about their own claim. A retailer can add a custom calculated attribute, such as each customer's total orders in the past year, to a loyalty email so every customer sees their own count. Developers can pass these values when they render a

title: Amazon S3 Storage Lens now tracks S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers
summary: Amazon S3 Storage Lens now provides storage metrics for each S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tier. You can see object counts and storage bytes in every tier across your buckets. This helps you track how your data moves between tiers, estimate storage costs, and measure your savings. S3 Storage Lens gives you visibility across your organization into storage usage and activity to help you optimize costs and performance. Access tier metrics appear in your S3 Storage Lens dashboards and metrics exports alongside your existing metrics. S3 Storage Lens also now publishes prefix metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management, so you can allocate shared bucket costs to teams and applications with split cost allocation data for S3. To get started, enable access tier metrics in your S3 Storage Lens advanced tier configuration. title: Amazon ECR now replicates image deletions across regions and accounts
summary: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports replicating image deletions and tag removals to your replication destinations. Previously, ECR replication copied images to destination regions and accounts but did not replicate deletions, requiring you to manage deletions separately in each location. With replication of deletes, your destination repositories stay consistent with the source automatically. Teams running multi-region or multi-account architectures no longer need to script or manually track image cleanup across every destination. When you delete an image or remove a tag in your source registry, whether directly or through a lifecycle policy, ECR propagates that deletion to each destination in the replication rule. Replicated deletions emit EventBridge events and are recorded in CloudTrail, so you have the same visibility into deletions as you do for image pushes. title: Amazon EBS now supports associating additional KMS keys with snapshots
summary: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) now supports associating additional AWS Key Management Service (KMS) keys with EBS snapshots. This new capability enables you to share and copy encrypted snapshots across accounts without first re-encrypting them, simplifying your disaster recovery and backup workflows. Customers use EBS snapshots as durable, point-in-time backups of EBS volumes. By associating an additional customer-managed KMS key (CMK) with a snapshot encrypted with an AWS managed key (AMK), for example, you enable cross-account sharing for that snapshot without re-encrypting its data. This feature accelerates your disaster recovery workflows and enhances operational efficiency for enterprise backup administrators and disaster recovery teams. Support for associating additional KMS keys with Amazon EBS snapshots is available in all AWS commercial, China, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) Regions, plus AWS Local Zones and AWS Outposts. title: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search combining vector and full text for more relevant search results
summary: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with full-text search within a single query. By combining semantic meaning and exact term matching into a single ranked list of results, hybrid search captures both intent and precise terms for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agent memory, and search applications. This can deliver more relevant ranked results than either method alone. Hybrid search works with the same S3 Vectors APIs and maintains subsecond latency for infrequent queries and latency around 100 milliseconds or less for frequent queries. S3 Vectors is designed to provide the same elasticity, durability, and availability as Amazon S3, and it reduces the total costs of storing and querying vectors by up to 90% compared to alternative vector solutions. With hybrid search, customers can now store the data that they want to make full-text searchable alongside the vectors. Customers write data with the PutVectors API as they do today and

title: Amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg
summary: Amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, automatic write-conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg tables. You can run multi-step, concurrent transformation pipelines directly on Iceberg tables and audit the results, with the transaction semantics you expect from a data warehouse. This helps anyone writing to Iceberg tables at production scale. Batch jobs get all-or-nothing commits across multiple steps. Streaming and scheduled jobs can write to the same tables at the same time. Analysts, auditors, and AI agents can query a table as it existed at any point in time. With multi-statement transactions, you group several statements in a single BEGIN…COMMIT statement and publish them as one atomic Iceberg snapshot. This means a multi-step load such as a MERGE followed by a DELETE, can be commited together as one atomic operation, are never queryable in a half-applied state, and roll back cleanly if there's a failure. title: Amazon Connect Health medical coding is now available in public preview
summary: Today, AWS announces the public preview of medical coding in Amazon Connect Health , a HIPAA-eligible AI service that works alongside healthcare teams across patient engagement and point-of-care workflows. Medical coding uses existing clinical documentation to suggest ICD-10-CM and CPT codes, including E&M levels and modifiers, for a provider or coder to review and approve before submission. You can integrate medical coding into your EHR or billing application through the Amazon Connect Health SDK, or use it with Amazon Connect Health ambient documentation. Each code links to the evidence that supports it and carries a confidence score, so reviewers can confirm a code before a claim goes out. In this public preview, you can choose to upload your organization's previously coded encounters, and the service builds a coding reference set specific to your organization. The corrections coders make feed that reference set and improve future coding suggestions. Medical coding is available in p

title: Amazon Connect Customer agent assist now supports interactive responses
summary: Amazon Connect Customer agent assist now supports interactive components, including cards, carousels, buttons, and input fields. The AI agent analyzes conversation context in real time, recommends actions, retrieves information, and executes tasks on behalf of contact center agents using MCP tools in Connect Customer or third-party services. Interactive responses let agents review information, provide details, select options, and confirm actions without manually typing a separate request for each action. The AI agent can also recommend step-by-step guides, cases, customer profiles, and third-party applications that agents can open with one click. For example, when a customer calls to dispute a charge, the AI agent can dynamically generate an interactive list of the customer’s recent transactions. The agent can select the disputed transaction, provide or confirm the required details, and approve the action. The AI agent can then use a connected tool to create the dispute request and dis

title: Set up, connect, and govern AI agents faster with Amazon WorkSpaces
summary: Building AI agents has become essential. Across your organization, teams want agents to handle ERP transactions, work through a claims queue, and operate the same applications your people use every day. But how do you move from experiments to production? Before an agent touches real systems and real data, you need to verify who it acted on behalf of, what it did, and whether it stayed within the limits you set. Without that visibility, the agent stays stuck in testing, and the value is never realized. Earlier this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents , extending the power and security of a cloud work environment to agents, not just people. Today, we're excited to announce new capabilities that make it even easier to operate agents confidently across your enterprise and move them from proof of concept to governed production in fewer steps. You can set up new agents or connect the ones your builders have already built, run them under your own identity providers and policies,

title: AWS KMS now supports key sharing with AWS Resource Access Manager
summary: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and users. You can now let trusted parties define the access they need through reusable managed permissions in RAM, while keeping full control of your keys and key policies. To share a key, create a resource share by selecting the keys to share, choosing a managed permission, and specifying the principals. You can use AWS managed permissions for common scenarios, or customer managed permissions (CMPs) authored by you or by trusted parties such as SaaS providers and central security teams. Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain. The trusted parties who need access to your keys can publish the policy once as a CMP, without the need for you to modify the key policies by hand. Y

title: AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities
summary: AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities in the MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage APIs. Previously, AWS Marketplace sellers reported usage to both APIs in whole numbers, and now they can report usage with up to six decimal places. Sellers can price and meter in the units that match how customers consume their product, for example reporting 1.5 terabytes (TB) of storage instead of 1 or 2 TB. To report decimal quantities, sellers use the new UsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter in MeterUsage and QuantityAsDecimal parameter in BatchMeterUsage, and existing integrations that report whole numbers continue to work without changes. Usage allocations, which split reported usage into buckets by tags, also support decimal quantities with the new AllocatedUsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter. This new feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace Metering Service is available. To learn more, see MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage in the AWS Marketplace API Reference

title: IAM Identity Center now supports VPC endpoints and network access controls
summary: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports interface VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink and network access controls, enabling you to keep IAM Identity Center traffic private and restrict which networks can reach your IAM Identity Center services. Previously, IAM Identity Center rejected traffic arriving through VPC endpoints, requiring all sign-in and API traffic to use public endpoints. With this launch, you can create interface VPC endpoints for AWS access portal and service APIs to route traffic over the AWS private network. IAM Identity Center sign-in traffic flows through the AWS Sign-in VPC endpoint. You can attach VPC endpoint policies to each endpoint to scope which AWS organizations, accounts and resources are reachable through your private connection. Network access controls add a second layer of enforcement at the IAM Identity Center instance level. When enabled, you can require that all access arrive through a VPC endpoint, allow specific IP address ranges or VPCs as truste

title: AWS WAF advanced rate-based rules are now available in AWS GovCloud (US), Thailand, and Mexico
summary: AWS WAF advanced rate-based rules are now available in the Asia Pacific (Thailand), Mexico (Central), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. Customers in these Regions can now aggregate requests using custom keys and choose a 1 or 2 minute evaluation window in addition to the existing 5 and 10 minute options, the same capabilities already available in other AWS Regions. A rate-based rule counts requests and applies an action, such as Block or CAPTCHA, when the request rate exceeds a limit you set. Previously, rate-based rules in these Regions could aggregate requests only by IP address and used a 5 or 10 minute evaluation window. Now you can aggregate by request components such as HTTP headers, cookies, query strings, URI paths, HTTP methods, and label namespaces, and combine up to five of them into a composite key. For example, you can limit login attempts per IP address and User-Agent pair, or per session cookie, which helps against attacks spread across many IP

title: AWS Security Hub now detects when vulnerable software is running on Amazon EC2 instances
summary: AWS Security Hub now detects when software with a known vulnerability is actively running on your Amazon EC2 instances. Exposure findings now include a new trait, *The EC2 instance is running software with a known vulnerability*. These findings get a higher severity rating than findings for the same vulnerability where the software isn't running. This helps your security team focus on the vulnerabilities that pose the greatest risk, without investing time and resources to investigate if the software is actually in use. Security teams managing thousands of instances can now prioritize patching based on actual runtime risk. Security Hub correlates data from Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring and Amazon Inspector VM Scanner to detect running vulnerable software. It then combines this with other signals to generate exposure findings for EC2 resources that may be at risk, so you can prioritize response and remediation. This capability is available at no additional cost with the AWS Securit

title: AWS Security Hub Network Scanning now supports scanning Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) database instances
summary: AWS Security Hub Network Scanning now scans Amazon RDS DB instances to identify those that are reachable from the internet. Network Scanning automatically discovers existing and new RDS DB instances in your accounts and scans each instance that has Public Access configured. For each reachable port associated with a DB instance, Security Hub creates a finding with details about the instance and the reachable port. RDS scanning gives you more visibility into which resources in your environment are reachable from the internet. You can then investigate and update their access settings as needed. RDS scanning is turned on automatically for all customers who already have Network Scanning enabled. Network Scanning probes your resources from the internet to detect reachability, beyond what security group rules and route tables suggest. Security Hub Exposures then correlates these findings with other findings and resource configurations to assess broader risk. Existing Security Hub customers ca

title: AWS Secrets Manager adds managed external secrets support for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks
summary: AWS Secrets Manager now supports managed external secrets for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks. Long-lived credentials that are not rotated increase the risk of unauthorized access if exposed. Rotating a third-party credential requires coordinated updates to the external service and every application that uses it. You set a rotation schedule from the AWS Management Console or API. Secrets Manager rotates the credential and stores the current value without a custom rotation Lambda function. Secrets Manager offers self-rotation and administrator-assisted rotation for Auth0 credentials. With self-rotation, the target application replaces its own secret. With administrator-assisted rotation, a separate Auth0 application with Management API permissions replaces the target application's secret. title: AWS Network Firewall now supports context-aware rules with AWS Transit Gateway-attached firewalls
summary: AWS Network Firewall attached to AWS Transit Gateway now allows you to use context-aware rules in your firewall policy. Network Firewall is a managed firewall and intrusion prevention service that inspects and filters traffic across your virtual private clouds (VPCs). With context-aware rules, you write rules that reference context from VPC resources instead of IP addresses. This makes it easier to apply consistent security controls as your organization grows. Existing rules automatically cover new workloads, so you don't need to update rules manually. Context-aware rules match traffic using VPCs, subnets, security groups, and Transit Gateway attachment identifiers, collectively known as context identifiers. You can reference context identifiers in a rule's source for any protocol, and in its destination for TCP-based protocols such as HTTP, TLS, and SSH. Flow and alert logs include context identifiers, so you can investigate activity based on context. Context-aware rules are available

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports ForceAuthn in SAML requests
summary: AWS IAM Identity Center now gives you the option to require workforce users to re-authenticate with your external identity provider (IdP) each time their user interactive session expires. By default, when a user's session expires, IAM Identity Center renews it through the user's existing IdP session, and the user isn't prompted to sign in again. For organizations with strict security or compliance requirements that mandate explicit user verification at regular intervals, this automatic renewal may not meet policy requirements. When you set user re-authentication to Required and a user's user interactive session expires, IAM Identity Center prompts the user to re-authenticate with your external IdP. This helps you enforce stronger sign-in controls for regulated workloads. IAM Identity Center implements this by adding the SAML 2.0 ForceAuthn attribute to the SAML request sent to your IdP. You can configure user re-authentication for any IAM Identity Center instance (organization or accou

title: AWS Backup adds logically air-gapped vault support for Amazon RDS
summary: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault now supports Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) DB instances. Logically air-gapped vaults are a type of AWS Backup vault that stores immutable, isolated backups, which are locked by default with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode. Secure sharing across accounts and AWS Organizations enables direct restore, reducing recovery time from a data loss event. You can now protect your Amazon RDS DB instances in logically air-gapped vaults. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default, and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys. This helps reduce the risk of downtime, ensure business continuity, and meet compliance requirements. To get started, use the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. Assign your RDS DB instances to a backup plan and specify a logically air-gapped vault in the same AWS Region as the copy destination. Share the vault for r

title: AWS announces Networking Flexible Cost Allocation for Amazon VPC
summary: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) now supports Networking Flexible Cost Allocation (FCA), which splits shared networking costs by the resources that actually drive them, so you can see what each team or application used. Until now, AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR), including CUR 2.0 in AWS Data Exports, showed networking usage as a single item, and most customers split it across teams with custom scripts and manual estimates. FCA splits this line item by the resources that generated it. It supports NAT gateway data processing and data transfer, including traffic to the internet, and in-Region Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and VPC peering data transfer. Today, when several teams share a resource such as a NAT gateway, the account that owns it pays the full cost and can't see which team or application drove it. To work around this, some customers built custom scripts to analyze VPC Flow Logs, which takes ongoing engineering effort. Others used fixed-percentage splits, which o

title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports KV cache-aware routing for real-time inference endpoints
summary: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports KV cache-aware routing for real-time inference endpoints, enabling you to reduce time to first token for LLM workloads with long or repeated prompts. Serving engines such as vLLM store the computed key-value (KV) cache for repeated prompt starts such as shared system prompts, documents, and conversation history, to skip repeated work. Across several instances, a request that lands where the cache is missing recomputes it. Under high load, instances also evict cached blocks to free GPU memory, including shared prompts and earlier conversation turns. KV cache-aware routing sends each request to the instance that holds the longest matching part of its prompt in cache. The vLLM container reports the cache blocks it stores and evicts, and SageMaker routes with that live view. If the lookup is slow or finds no match, the endpoint falls back to load-aware routing, so the request is still served. Prefix-aware routing suits stable shared prompts, short prompts,

title: AgentCore runtime instances are now available in six more AWS Regions
summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances are now available in six additional AWS Regions: US West (N. California), Canada (Central), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Seoul). Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. By expanding to these AWS Regions, more teams can use runtime instance capabilities such as GPU-accelerated, memory-optimized, or compute-optimized instance types, and long-running agent sessions of up to 14 days. You can run your agents closer to your users to reduce invocation latency, and keep agent instances, storage volumes, and session data in the Region that your data residency requirements call for. With this expansion, you can use runtime instances in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London)

title: Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration now supported in CloudFormation
summary: Aurora PostgreSQL now supports express configuration in AWS CloudFormation for infrastructure as code deployment. This launch enables you to automate the infrastructure deployment of your Aurora clusters through CloudFormation templates while benefiting from the speed of express configuration. Aurora PostgreSQL clusters created with express configuration allow you to create and query an Aurora serverless database in seconds. The new withExpressConfiguration createOnly property on the AWS::RDS::DBCluster resource creates both the cluster and its primary database instance from one property declaration. You don't need to model or manage the instance separately in your CloudFormation template. This simplifies your templates and makes it easier to manage Aurora clusters with express configuration through infrastructure as code. The CloudFormation support is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora PostgreSQL with express configuration is offered. To learn more, see the Aurora User Guide an

title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports centralized configuration with AWS Organizations declarative policies
summary: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports AWS Organizations declarative policies. You can use them to enable Security Hub CSPM across all accounts and Regions in your organization and to define which security standards and controls are enabled. Policies can apply broadly to every account and Region, or target specific account and Region combinations. Declarative policies help keep each account's configuration aligned with its attached policy, which helps prevent configuration drift. You can also apply them automatically to new accounts, so each account starts with a baseline configuration as soon as it's created. Declarative policies are now the recommended way to manage Security Hub CSPM across an organization. They align with how other security services, such as Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, and AWS Security Hub allow customers to manage configuration of the service. They also provide more flexibility, such as configuring Region-specific settings. You can continue to use central confi

title: AWS Secrets Manager now supports cross-account replication
summary: AWS Secrets Manager now supports cross-account replication, enabling you to maintain a synchronized copy of a primary secret in a secondary AWS account for cross-account access, backup, and disaster recovery. Cross-account replication extends the existing multi-Region replication capability across account boundaries. With cross-account replication, platform or security teams can own and rotate a secret centrally, and each consuming account gets a local, always-current copy without any shared KMS keys or cross-account secret policies. The replica secret is a full, independent resource, encrypted with a customer managed KMS key owned by the replica account. Secrets Manager updates it automatically whenever the primary secret's value changes, including rotations. You can keep a live copy of critical secrets in a dedicated recovery or failover account, isolated from ransomware or a compromised primary account. If needed, the replica can be promoted to a standalone secret. Cross-account rep

title: AWS Marketplace now supports VAT credit notes for deemed supply refunds
summary: AWS Marketplace sellers can now submit Value Added Tax (VAT) credit notes for refunded deemed supply transactions through a self-service experience in AWS Partner Central. Previously, VAT was disbursed to sellers for eligible transactions, and when a buyer was later refunded, sellers had to contact AWS to submit the corresponding credit note. This launch simplifies post-refund VAT documentation for sellers. Sellers can view eligible refund line items in the VAT on deemed supply section, select the refunds covered by a credit note, upload a PDF or the applicable electronic invoice format, and track the submission status. Sellers can consolidate multiple eligible refunds into a single credit note where applicable and review the associated financial adjustment in the Seller Insights reporting. These capabilities are available for eligible AWS Marketplace transactions, including Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO) transactions, in supported EU member states, Norway, and the United Kingdom

title: AWS Batch on Amazon EKS adds Linux capabilities, seccomp, and pod-level settings
summary: AWS Batch now supports additional Kubernetes security context settings in Amazon EKS job definitions, including Linux capabilities, seccomp profiles, and pod-level settings. For EKS clusters that enforce the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards restricted profile, you can now run AWS Batch jobs with only the privileges and system calls they require. To get started, use the RegisterJobDefinition API to set capabilities and seccompProfile in a container's securityContext , or set securityContext in podProperties to define pod-wide settings such as fsGroup . Container-level settings override pod-level defaults. You can configure these settings through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. The additional security context settings for AWS Batch on Amazon EKS are now supported in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see the Amazon EKS properties section in the AWS Batch User Guide .

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports layout customization for designations
summary: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports layout customization, a new capability that gives domain administrators control over which tools and left navigation items project members see based on their designation. Organizations with data engineering, analytics, and machine learning teams on a single platform can configure a layout within each designation definition, and that layout applies across every project in the domain without per-project configuration. Previously, all project members saw the same interface regardless of their role, creating confusion and potential governance issues. With layout customization, administrators define a layout as part of a designation that specifies which left navigation items are visible for project members assigned to that designation. When a project member opens a project, SageMaker Unified Studio resolves the member's designation and renders only the tools included in their designation's layout. For example, a SQL analyst designation can be con

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports OAuth 2.0 discovery URLs
summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs for both inbound JWT authorization and outbound OAuth credential providers. This update enables developers to configure AgentCore with OAuth 2.0 authorization servers that do not use OpenID Connect (OIDC). Previously, AgentCore Identity accepted only OIDC discovery URLs. Authorization servers that implement OAuth 2.0 without OIDC publish their metadata at a different well-known path and could not be used with AgentCore. With this launch, you can use either OIDC or OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs when you configure a JWT authorizer or a custom OAuth credential provider on AgentCore. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is available, at no additional cost. To learn more, see Configure inbound JWT authorizer and Add OAuth client using custom provider in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide .

title: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange
summary: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693). Amazon Cognito helps you add sign-up, sign-in, and access control to your web applications, mobile applications, and AI agents. With token exchange, a service or AI agent acting on a user's behalf can exchange the user's token for a new token scoped to a specific downstream service. Previously, a service that called another service on a user's behalf had to forward the user's original token or build and maintain its own token minting logic. With token exchange, you can issue a new token that has a narrower scope than the original token, is bound to a single audience, and comes without a refresh token. When you include an actor token, Cognito adds an act claim that identifies the intermediary, so downstream services can tell a request that an agent made on a user's behalf from one the user made directly. For example, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server can exchange a user's token for a narrowly scoped token to call a bac

title: CVE-2026-126793 - Privilege escalation in Aurora PostgreSQL dialect detection in AWS Advanced Go Wrapper
summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-182-AWS Publication Date: 11/12/2026 13:00 PM PST Description: An untrusted search path issue in Aurora PostgreSQL dialect detection in the AWS Advanced Go Wrapper from release 2026-04-06 (awssql/v2.0.0) and before release 2026-07-29 (awssql/v2.0.3) could allow a remote authenticated user to escalate privileges to those of another database user, including a member of the rds_superuser role, via a crafted function that runs when that user connects to an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster through an affected version of the wrapper. Impacted versions: AWS Advanced Go Wrapper >=2026-04-06, <2026-07-29 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.

title: CVE-2026-127119 - Unverified ownership of the default EMR cluster log location in AWS SDK for pandas
summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-181-AWS Publication Date: 11/12/2026 13:00 PM PST Description: We identified CVE-2026-127119, an issue in the EMR module of AWS SDK for pandas (awswrangler) from version 1.1.0 before 3.18.0. When a cluster is created without an explicit log location, the library uses a predictable default S3 bucket name for the cluster logs without verifying that the caller's account owns that bucket. A remote actor who creates that bucket first could read the cluster's logs, including job step output. Impacted versions: >= 1.1.0 AND < 3.18.0 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.

title: Amazon Aurora and RDS now support Graviton5-based R9g database instances
summary: AWS Graviton5-based R9g database instances are now generally available for Amazon Aurora with PostgreSQL compatibility and MySQL compatibility, and for Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MariaDB. Graviton5-based R9g instances provide up to a 30% performance improvement and up to a 22% price-performance improvement for on-demand pricing over Graviton4-based instances of equivalent sizes on Amazon Aurora, depending on database engine, version, and workload. Built on the AWS Nitro System, R9g instances are available in nine sizes, from large to 48xlarge. They deliver up to 192 vCPUs, an 8:1 ratio of memory to vCPU, up to 100 Gbps of networking bandwidth, and up to 72 Gbps of bandwidth to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). You can get started using the R9g database instances through the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI). The instances are available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Frankfurt) regions. For the

title: Amazon MWAA now supports fine-grained access control with IAM Identity Center and multi-team environments
summary: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) now supports fine-grained access control, giving administrators precise control over who can access which workflows and resources in an Apache Airflow environment. Fine-grained access control is delivered through two new capabilities: IAM Identity Center integration and multi-team environments. With IAM Identity Center integration, users sign in to the Apache Airflow UI with their corporate identity provider. Authorization is evaluated per request using IAM policies attached to IAM Identity Center Permission Sets, with condition keys that scope access by resource type (DAGs, connections, variables, pools, and more), action, and specific resource ID. With multi-team environments, several teams can share a single MWAA environment. Each team gets its own DAG folder in Amazon S3, and users see only shared DAGs plus their own teams' DAGs based on IAM Identity Center group membership. Teams reduce cost through shared infrastructure an

title: Amazon Connect Customer supports merging and linking related cases in the agent workspace
summary: Amazon Connect Customer now lets agents merge and link related cases in the agent workspace, so they can resolve customer issues faster and respond consistently. When a customer contacts a business about the same issue more than once, or on different channels, the history can end up split across several cases. Agents can merge those cases into one case with a single, consolidated history. For example, an agent can merge the chat and email cases a customer opened about a delayed shipment. Agents can also link related cases, such as cases from different customers affected by the same issue, so they can coordinate one consistent response for every affected customer. Cases is available in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documen

title: Amazon SNS now supports push notifications in four additional AWS Regions
summary: Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) now supports sending push notifications in the Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Europe (Zurich), and AWS GovCloud (US-East) Regions. Amazon SNS is a fully managed pub/sub service that provides message delivery to multiple endpoints, including AWS Lambda, Amazon SQS, Amazon Data Firehose, HTTP, SMS (via AWS End User Messaging), push notifications, and email. With this launch, customers in these four additional Regions can use Amazon SNS to send push notifications to the following supported push notification services: Amazon Device Messaging (ADM), Apple Push Notification Service (APNs), Baidu Cloud Push (Baidu), Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), and Windows Push Notification Services (WNS). For the full list of Regions from which you can send push notifications, see Supported Regions and Countries in the Amazon SNS Developer Guide. For more information, see the Amazon SNS push notifications documentation .

title: EC2 Image Builder console now integrates with the DevOps Agent for troubleshooting and resource creation
summary: EC2 Image Builder now integrates with the AWS DevOps Agent directly in the Image Builder console, enabling you to troubleshoot failed image pipelines and create resources directly from the console chat panel. You can diagnose up to 50 failed pipelines at once and ask follow-up questions in the same conversation. You can also choose to create resources by describing what you want, and the agent populates the console with values the service has already validated. With this integration, diagnosing a failed pipeline no longer requires manually inspecting build logs, cross-referencing error codes, or iterating through configuration fixes, saving you significant time and expertise. The agent reads build logs, workflow steps, components, and network configuration, then provides the root cause and the steps to fix it. For resource creation, the agent verifies the configuration before populating the console for you to review and submit. If you troubleshoot or build with your own AI agents, the

title: AWS Glue announces automatic version upgrades for Apache Spark jobs
summary: AWS Glue introduces automatic version upgrades, a capability that keeps your Apache Spark jobs current on the latest AWS Glue runtime without manual coordination. Staying current on supported runtimes gives your jobs the latest security patches, performance improvements, and support for evolving table formats such as Apache Iceberg. Auto upgrades include multiple levels of validations including assessing jobs for compatibility with the upgraded runtime, obtaining your consent before executing jobs on a newer version, and validating upgraded job runs against each job's established output profile, so your jobs upgrade with the right guardrails in place. By setting a job's version to "Auto", upgrades that once required weeks of planning and execution now happen automatically. Platform teams can standardize runtime versions across large fleets without chasing individual job owners, and business units without a central upgrade team can keep their jobs current hands-free. Each job is validat

title: AWS Cloud WAN now supports BGP communities on Direct Connect attachments for routing policy
summary: AWS Cloud WAN now supports BGP communities on Direct Connect attachments, enabling advanced routing controls for enterprise hybrid networks. Previously, Cloud WAN Routing Policy evaluated BGP communities only on Site-to-Site VPN and Connect attachments. Now, customers can tag routes with routing intent on-premises, apply filtering and path preference rules inside Cloud WAN, and propagate communities back to their on-premises routers over Direct Connect. With this capability, enterprises can simplify hybrid network orchestration by signaling routing policies dynamically from on-premises environments. Customers can match community tags to filter production versus disaster recovery traffic, prioritize preferred paths, or restrict regional propagation. This eliminates the need for VPN overlay workarounds and manual policy replication, reducing operational complexity and misconfiguration risk. BGP community support on AWS Cloud WAN Direct Connect attachments is available in all AWS Regions

title: AWS Backup now supports resource modifiers for Amazon EKS restores
summary: Today, AWS Backup announces support for resource modifiers when restoring Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) backups. Resource modifiers let you transform Kubernetes resources during a restore, so you can adapt a restored cluster to its target environment. When you restore an EKS backup that has been copied across accounts or across AWS Regions, the restored cluster can carry references tied to the source environment, such as IAM roles, database endpoints, and Amazon ECR registry URIs. Previously, you had to locate and update these references manually after every restore, which was time consuming and error prone. With resource modifiers, you can define transformation rules once via a YAML file, and AWS Backup applies them automatically as part of the restore, improving the reliability of your cross-account and cross-Region disaster recovery workflows. AWS Backup support for resource modifiers for Amazon EKS backups is available in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud

title: AWS Backup adds logically air-gapped vault support for Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive
summary: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault now supports Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive. Logically air-gapped vaults are a type of AWS Backup vault that allows secure sharing of backups across accounts and AWS Organizations, supporting direct restore to reduce recovery time from a data loss event. You can now archive Amazon EBS backups held in a logically air-gapped vault to Amazon EBS Snapshots Archive, a low-cost tier for snapshots you rarely access. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default, and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys. This helps you meet long-term retention and compliance requirements at lower storage cost. You can get started using the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. In a backup plan rule that runs monthly or less often, specify a logically air-gapped vault as the primary backup destination or copy destination. Then enable Archive Amazon EBS snapshots in the backup rul

title: Amazon Route 53 now supports record set protection
summary: Amazon Route 53 now supports record set protection, which helps DNS administrators prevent accidental changes to critical DNS records in their hosted zones. This feature allows you to protect records such as those at the zone apex, MX records, and production endpoints directly in the hosted zone. Any change to a protected record is blocked until the protection is removed by an authorized user. Previously, to lock specific records, you had to write record-level conditions into the IAM policies of every user and role that could change your hosted zones. When those policies blocked a change, the caller had no indication of whether the record was protected or why. Now you can protect records by name and type directly in the hosted zone. A single protection covers all records with that name and type, including records with different set identifiers; weighted, latency, and other routing policy records are protected together. You can also create a protection proactively before the record exis

title: Amazon Route 53 Domains now supports self-service restore for expired and deleted domains
summary: Amazon Route 53 Domains now lets you restore an expired or recently deleted domain yourself, using the Amazon Route 53 console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Previously, restoring a domain required a request to AWS Support. Now you can recover a domain lost to a missed renewal, an expired payment method, or an accidental deletion, and restore the website, email, and applications that depend on it. To restore a domain, you enter the domain name, review the restoration price, accept the charge, and submit the request. Route 53 works with the top-level domain (TLD) registry to reactivate the registration and return the domain to your AWS account. Most TLD registries support restoration, and each registry sets how long after expiration or deletion a domain can still be restored. Restoring a domain typically costs more than registering or renewing one. To learn more, see Restoring an expired or deleted domain in the Route 53 Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page . For a complet

title: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink introduces enhanced snapshots
service: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
summary: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink now supports enhanced snapshots, a capability that lets you capture, export, and restore application state across Apache Flink applications and AWS Regions, so you can run blue/green deployments, easily migrate self-managed workloads to Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink without losing state, and keep backup in a secondary Region for cross-Region recovery. To deploy an application update without pausing processing for blue/green deployments, create an enhanced snapshot from an application and use it to start a second application. To migrate a self-managed workload, import its Apache Flink savepoint into Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink as an enhanced snapshot. For cross-Region recovery, export an enhanced snapshot to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and replicate the exported state to a bucket in a secondary Region. Enhanced snapshots are available today for applications on Apache Flink 1.20 and later in all AWS Re

title: Amazon FSx for Lustre now offers a 75% lower minimum throughput capacity and metadata IOPS for Intelligent-Tiering file systems
summary: Amazon FSx for Lustre is reducing the minimum provisioned throughput capacity and metadata IOPS on Intelligent-Tiering file systems by 75%, allowing you to use Intelligent-Tiering even more cost-effectively for high-performance computing (HPC) and machine learning workloads that start with small datasets and grow over time. The FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering storage class delivers the lowest-cost and only fully elastic Lustre file storage in the cloud. It is optimized for workloads that mix hot and cold data and do not require consistent SSD-level performance. A file system's throughput capacity determines the read and write speeds supported by its underlying file servers, and its level of metadata IOPS determines how many files and directories you can create, read, and delete per second. Today’s launch reduces the minimum throughput capacity on an Intelligent-Tiering file system from 4,000 to 1,000 MBps and the minimum metadata performance from 6,000 to 1,500 IOPS. The lower throu

title: Amazon FSx for Lustre lowers the entry cost of Intelligent-Tiering file systems by 75%
summary: Amazon FSx for Lustre is reducing the minimum provisioned throughput capacity and metadata IOPS on Intelligent-Tiering file systems by 75%, allowing you to use Intelligent-Tiering even more cost-effectively for high-performance computing (HPC) and machine learning workloads that start with small datasets and grow over time. The FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering storage class delivers the lowest-cost and only fully elastic Lustre file storage in the cloud.
